en: Oṃ, homage to Vāgīśvara.
Having prostrated with my three bodies before the Supreme,
who is equal to space, I compose this commentary on the *Khasama-tantra*, which is like space itself, for the sake of that [Supreme] reality.

In this context, the Blessed One Vajradhara is the enlightenment (*bodhi*) of all Buddhas. That [enlightenment] is characterized by the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*). The basis is the body, and it is threefold for them. Among these, as long as the basis characterized by the continuum of mind remains the support for the seeds of defiled phenomena and their latencies—which are called "dysfunction" (*dauṣṭulya*)—it is designated as the "storehouse" (*ālaya*). Subsequently, through the Noble Path that is free from conceptual proliferation and has been cultivated for a long time, because those [seeds and latencies] are completely exhausted, there arises the state designated as "non-storehouse" (*anālaya*), which is the foundation.

The restriction of cessation consists in the disappearance of those representations appearing as body and enjoyments, as well as other afflicted phenomena—both those that have arisen and those that have not yet arisen—and in their absolute non-arising in that form. However, the restriction of activity, which is the revolution of the basis (*parāvṛtti*), consists in the manifestation of an infinite, non-conceptual nature of luminosity that is like the pure sky. This is the Buddhas' revolution of the basis of the latent predispositions of corruption (*dauṣṭhulya*).

That very [basis] is called their untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*), because it is the seed-basis for the untainted Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*). That path (*mārga*) is also their support (*āśraya*). Its revolution (*parāvṛtti*) consists of the absolute cessation of the mundane form and the absolute activity of the supramundane form. The suchness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-tathatā*) is also their support. Its revolution is the absolute purification from all adventitious obscurations.

That which is the revolution (*parāvṛtti*) of the Buddhas' basis of corruption, their basis of the path, and their basis of suchness (*tathatā*)—that alone is their awakening (*bodhi*), and that alone is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Because it is the body, the support, of the Buddha-qualities, it is also called the "essential body" (*svābhāvikakāya*), since it abides eternally in the very nature of suchness and its manifestation. Thus, this Blessed One Vajradhara, characterized by the awakening of a Buddha, is by nature equal to space.

The *prakṛti* (nature) is his natural body (*svābhāvikakāya*); by virtue of that, it is indeed equal to space, because its intrinsic nature is suchness (*tathatā*), which consists of appearances that are non-manifesting, infinite, and perfectly pure. Although the enjoyment body (*sāṃbhogikakāya*) is not equal to space in its various forms due to the diversity of its aspects, nevertheless, in accordance with its manifestation, it is indeed equal to space. For the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) experiences phenomena unobstructed through its reality that is equal to space, and the enjoyment body likewise discerns them; this is because experience is without vibration.

And how does it determine them in such a way? By determining that the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and their appearances do not exist. For example, the determination of ordinary people, which results from the experience of jars and so forth, [determines them] by way of their existence.

Just as the vivid experience of a jar-form in fools, even without the verbalization of "existence," determines it as existing through the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) from previous habituation to certainty, so too the non-conceptual *saṃbhogakāya* of the Buddhas determines its own form as non-existent. This very determination is what is intended here by the term "manifestation" (*pratibhāsa*). For manifestation is of two kinds: direct experience (*saṃvedana*) and secondary indication (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Therefore, even the *saṃbhogakāya* of the Buddhas is, according to its appearance, equal to space. The *nirmāṇakāya*, however, is all the more equal to space, because even illusionists discern that a person or other entity created by themselves lacks any real existence. And that Vajradhara is the progenitor of all Buddhas; they too are equal to space because they are his emanations—this is the established tenet.

Regarding this established doctrine (*siddhānta*), an objection is raised: Vajradhara is certainly not the progenitor of the Buddhas; rather, he is a son of the Buddhas because he wears the crown of the five Buddhas. Due to his union with their body, speech, and mind, as well as with that circle of goddesses (*devīcakra*), he is merely a conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and the one who sets in motion the method of proliferation. He is neither like space nor the one who sets in motion the method of being like space. To refute this objection, it is said: "The five Buddhas," and so forth. Here are two verses on this point:
"In this world, there are groups consisting of two, three, four, five, or six measures, categorized in five ways."
Generally, the *dvipadī* meter consists of a foot formed by three or four *gaṇas*.
In this context, Apabhraṃśa is a dialect and a modification of Saṃskṛta;
its completion is achieved through short and long vowels, the bindu, and the fast and slow tempos.

*Dvipadī-khaṇḍa* is a synonym for *vastuka*. In that [meter], in the first *dvipādikā*, there are three groups (*gaṇas*) of feet. In the odd-numbered [feet], the first group consists of six morae (*mātras*), the second consists of two morae, and the remaining [groups] consist of four morae each. The word "ca" (and) has its *ca* elided and is displaced in the sequence. There are two instances of the word "ho. One is a substitute for "usa"; the second is an indeclinable used in the sense of "indeed" (*khalu*) or as a vocative. The shortening of the vowel *o* in the word "ho" is for the purpose of metrical completion.

For instance, in Apabhraṃśa, there is shortening [of vowels], as in *arddakhepa* for *ardrakṣepa*; and the substitution of *e* and *o* occurs according to observation when joined with other letters, as in *jai ke vi*, *jai ko vi*, and *jai pi u*. In that context, the connection is as follows: "He whose crown is the locus of the five Buddhas, and whose essence is the three worlds—or rather, the world of women—and who possesses the nature established by Ādibuddha; his movement is indeed equal to space (*khasama*). The term *mukhṭāśrayā* means "residing in the crown" (*mukuṭasthā*); "whose" refers to Vajrasattva.

The three secrets of body, speech, and mind are subsumed within the mandala of the yogins. Alternatively, "strī" (woman) refers to the *yoginīs*; their world (*bhuvana*) is the mandala, which is the "woman-world" (*strībhuvana*). That which has this as its essence and its manifestation is [the Vajra-yāna], because it is the nature of the vajra. As it is said in the *Śrī-guhyasamāja*: "In delusion, hatred, and passion, delight is always established in the vajra. It is known as the Vajra-yāna, the means of all Buddhas. (Guhyasamāja 18.52)
Delusion, hatred, and likewise passion—delight always resides in the vajra;
therefore, it is known as the Vajrayāna of the Buddhas, for it is their skillful means.

Because he is the first of the six *cakravartins*, Vajrasattva is the *Ādibuddha*. Precisely because he is a *cakravartin*, he is made to possess a crown (*samukuṭa*) and a maṇḍala; thus he is so called because he possesses this produced (*kṛtaka*), conventional (*sāṃvṛta*) state. For one who exists in such a manner, whatever this activity (*pracāra*) or worldly convention (*vyavahāra*)—the conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) consisting of his own body, speech, mind, crown, Buddhas, and so forth—all of that is equal to space (*khasama*), because it appears by virtue of being equal to space. This is due to the determination [of them] through the non-existence of their forms.

Therefore, this Blessed One is himself equal to space, and he is the promulgator of the Vajra Way, which is equal to space. Even the conventional representation of the Buddhas upon his own crown was created by him alone; how much more so, then, the emanated Buddhas? Consequently, he alone is the progenitor of the Buddhas.

But is he not also called a son of the Buddha? How so? Because at times he possesses the form of a bodhisattva, and bodhisattvas are the sons of the Buddha. But surely, according to the Mantra system, the body, speech, and mind of the Blessed One, as well as the maṇḍala, are meditated upon. Therefore, there would be no attainment of the non-manifest Dharma-body (dharmakāya). If that is not attained, then the enjoyment and emanation bodies (saṃbhoga- and nirmāṇakāya), which depend upon it, would all the more remain unattained.

"Now, if its cultivation is indeed something else, let that be explained," he says with the words beginning "jai" (*yadi*). Here, the *gaṇas* consist of exactly four morae (*mātrās*): those on odd positions have four [morae], while those on even positions have three. Both "e" and "ai" are short *e*-vowels with a very small bindu. By means of this primordial state (*bhāva*), the mind is characterized. This state of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)—the very nature of the Buddha—is certainly not perceived as an object of sight, nor is it of the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

By this—meaning by what is to be stated in the second half [of the verse], namely, by the method of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*)—the mind of the yogin is examined and composed in samādhi. This is the meditation on the ultimate Vajrasattva; there is no other. Indeed, by what means is it not seen, not perceived, and not conceptualized? Nor is it an aspect that constitutes the intrinsic nature of consciousness, because it cannot withstand analysis as being either one or many. For thus, the non-perception of the grasped and the grasper is the cause for attaining the *dharmakāya*, which consists in the non-perception of duality.

The cultivation of body, speech, and mind, however, pertains to the two enjoyment bodies; therefore, this alone is their cultivation, because it leads more swiftly to the attainment of the three bodies.

Let it be that such is the meditation for Vajradhara; but how is it for the Buddhas and others? To this he says: "The Buddha," and so forth. Here, in each quarter there are four *gaṇas*; in the first quarter, the first two are of two and three morae respectively, beginning with a *yuk* (long syllable). The first [of these] is of six morae, the second is of two morae, and the remaining ones are of four morae each. For the Buddha, Vajradhara, Ratnaketu, and the one accompanied by Padma—among these deities, there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

The *Ādibuddha* has the nature of space (*ākāśasvabhāva*). "Of the Buddha" means of Vairocana; "of the Vajradhara" means of Akṣobhya; "of Ratnaketu" means of Ratnasambhava; "by Padma" means by Amitābha; "of Vṛtta" means of Karma [i.e., Amoghasiddhi]; such is the meaning. Regarding these five Tathāgatas, and regarding the gods, the goddesses, and the families, there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because both the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*) are unreal due to the illusory appearance of duality.

If the duality is false, what then is their own nature? "Ādibuddha" refers to Vajradhara. "Space" refers to that which is equal to space (*khasama*), because it has the characteristic of the *dharmakāya* and appears as being equal to space—this is their intrinsic nature.

He states "āi" and so forth in order to withdraw their own form because of their lack of movement (*niṣpanda*). Here too, there are four *gaṇas* per quarter; in the first quarter, the first [syllable] consists of six and two morae (*mātrās*) respectively; likewise in the fourth and third quarters, the first is of two morae and the remaining are of four morae each. Thus, in the case of "upajja," the doubling of the letter *pa* is not accepted.

*Khaiṃ*: [The syllable] *kha* is protracted, having three morae (*trimātra*). From the word *kha*, the suffix *ka* is added in the sense of the word itself (*svārthe*), resulting in the elision of the vowel and the retention of the final consonant. The third case singular ending becomes *ī*, and there is the elision of the letter *a*. This is the arising of the primordial phenomenon (*ādidharma*): sentient beings arise equal to space (*khena samānāḥ*). Although there is plurality, the singular number is employed according to the system; in this matter, the scripture is the authority. The primordial, pure state is equal to space. The primordial phenomenon is Vajrasattva, because his nature is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). His arising occurs through body, speech, and mind, which are equal to space.

Its arising is indeed its manifestation through the destruction of all obscurations without exception, like the "arising of space" upon the demolition of a palace. Space serves as the illustrative example for its arising. Thus it is said in the *Śrīparamādya*: "Because he is the sign of the arising of space, the Supreme Being (Satva) who consists of all vajras is without beginning or end; he is Vajrasatva, the supreme bliss."
Thus it is. For this very reason, sentient beings, Buddhas, and so forth arise, because they are delimited by the non-existence of [intrinsic] forms. They are equal to space.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that in the Yoga Tantras, the very accomplishment of Mahāmudrā is enlightenment? Its cause is knowledge equal to space (*khasama-jñāna*), but that is not its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, there is a contradiction between all the Yoga Tantras and the Tantra Equal to Space. To this, he says: "The method" (*naya*), and so forth. A "method" (*naya*) is that by which something is led or explained. That Blessed One by whom a sūtra of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*) is explained is the "method. Even if the intended meaning is not explicitly expressed in words, the scripture—the teaching of the Blessed One—is accepted as authoritative, but not that which is contrary to it.

Now, regarding the question: "What is the method (*naya*) concerning mantra, mudrā, and so forth, when knowledge (*jñāna*) possesses form? he says: "The primordial," and so on. "Primordial purity" (*ādiśuddha*) refers to the *dharmakāya* which is primordially pure. That itself is the "state" (*pada*), the objective support (*ālambana*), which is equal to space-like knowledge. Because [mantra, mudrā, etc.]—which are the natural outflow (*niṣpanda*) of that which is equal to space—appear as being equal to space, this is the *uttaratantra* (the higher tantra) of all tantras.
It is also said in the *Śrīsarvarahasyatantra*: "There is no causal reality whatsoever, and likewise no resultant reality."
That is reality, that is the knowledge of suchness; therein the yogi should practice.

Thus, the reality of the cause consists of the four aspects of the penetration of mind; the reality of the fruit consists of the [resultant] aspect. Both of these are non-existent as aspects; rather, the reality of those two is the very gnosis of suchness (*tathatājñāna*), because it discerns them through the non-existence of their own aspects. The meaning is that the yogi should practice within that discernment. It is also said in the *Śrīsamāja*: "The syllable of the body is unarisen; speech and mind are without characteristics."
"Arising from the conceptualization of the space-vajra, it is a false collection of collections" (Guhyasamāja 17.36).

It is called "immutable" (*akṣara*) because it does not perish; it is the secret—the secret of body, the secret of speech, and the secret of mind. All of that appears as unarisen and without intrinsic nature. Because of the delimitation through the non-existence of forms, within the space-vajra—the *dharmakāya* experienced as the duality of phenomena—it is a conceptualized entity consisting of delimitation. By means of the reality equal to space, there is delimitation through existence and through the non-existence of forms as they appear.

And that [knowledge] is false because it possesses mental aspects (*sākāra*); whereas "comprehension" (*saṃgraha*) is due to its correct discernment (*samyak-pariccheda*). Therefore, it is so called because it is "comprised" (*saṃgraha*) by that [correct discernment], meaning it is comprised by pure mundane knowledge (*śuddha-laukika-jñāna*). Thus, first of all, the meditation on the object as being like space, which is common to all Yoga Tantras, has been explained.

Now, in order to introduce the common meditation on the object of realization as being equal to space (*khasama*) according to the *Śrīsamāja* and other tantras, he says "five," and so forth. The two lines of two feet have the same metrical count as the first; the first word *ca* has the sense of "and" (*artha*), while the second has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) and is displaced in its sequence. One should pay homage to Vajrasattva, whose very nature is the Dharma even though he wears the crown of the five Buddhas, and who possesses the power of the Dharma throughout the three worlds.

Of what nature is he, even though embodied, who possesses as his very essence the *dharmakāya* of the five Buddhas? He is of such a nature because he is perceived in that form—the *dharmakāya* itself, which is equal to space and consists of all the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*) in a state of equal flavor (*samarasībhūta*). Furthermore, of what nature is he? The three worlds are the wheel of yoginīs (*yoginīcakra*). He is so described because his characteristic is the enjoyment of the Dharma (*dharmasaṃbhoga*), for the influence of the Dharma is the teaching of the Dharma. And it is said in the *Vajraśikhara*: "Then, from the essential bodies (*svābhāvikakāya*), he is again emanated through the enjoyments (*saṃbhoga*)."

Thus, in this context, it is meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) alone that is intended as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Prostration is the entry of one’s own body, speech, and mind into the body, speech, and mind of [the deity]. He states the benefit resulting from prostration with the words beginning "Vajra... and so forth. When Vajrasattva is being prostrated to, merit also becomes infinite. By prostrating to these [deities], the greatness of the Dharma and merit are obtained; by the word "also" (*api*), knowledge is also included. It is "infinite" to the extent that the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*) may become fully perfected.

Furthermore, let it be prostrated to again, for through prostration one obtains the greatness of the Dharma and the majesty of Vajradhara. In some manuscripts, the word *svabhāva* is read in place of *mahattva*; in that case, there would be an impossibility of the *yamaka* (rhyme/parallelism), which is a fault because of its deviation [from the intended meaning].

It has been stated that the *dharmakāya* itself attains the state of the body of Vajrasattva. In that regard, the *dharmakāya* has not yet been directly realized; it must be cultivated through symbolic means (*saṅketa*). He explains this with the words beginning with "all" (*sarva*) and so forth. This too is that same two-line verse, but by means of its two lines, having thoroughly permeated all sentient beings, liberation as its very nature is brought about.

Having summoned all the perfectly awakened ones with the sounds of illusory passion and caused them to enter, one visualizes them dissolving into the heart; having contemplated them as situated within the interior of a lotus, the nature of liberation is produced—the *dharmakāya*, which is the state of equal flavor (*samarasībhāva*) of all the qualities of a Buddha, white like the melting of the autumn moon.

To the question, "What is done after that? he says: "Vajra... and so forth. Here, the "four groups" refers to the four lines [of the verse]. Liberation is made to have the nature of all things through Vajrasattva; it is the nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*). And this phenomenon has an indestructible nature. If so, how is it then made into a body? To this he says: "By the world," and so forth. "By the world" means by way of cause; the meaning is "for the sake of the world."

Another nature in the form of Vajrasattva is produced and displayed, because it is recognized through the Vinaya according to convention by way of that transformation. However, in the ultimate sense, it is simply another cognition arising in that form—which is the natural outflow (*niṣyanda*) of the Dharmakāya—and the manifestation of the Blessed One occurs through its non-existence in accordance with that form. From this point onward, that same two-footed [meter] consists of three groups of syllables per foot. Prior to the rule *e ca u devī*, there is the rule *kā a* and so forth. Here, the shortness of the types of arising is for the purpose of filling [the meter].
Body, speech, and mind therein are the initial arising of the Dharma. The yoga-seat is where the goddess Cundā arises as the Dharma; in that generation of Vajrasattva, what is its arising?

If one asks what the place of origin is, he says: "Body, speech, and mind"—this triad is the primordial origin of the Dharma-Vajrasattva. The seat and foundation of yoga is the Blessed Lady Cundā Mahākāyā; within her occurs the birth of Vajrasattva. As for who his parents are and how his birth occurs, he says: "Vajjaho," and so forth. "Vajjaho" is a group of six morae (mātras) pronounced with a slow tempo (*vilambita*). Therein, the mantra-practitioner meditates upon the single-natured [deity] of the Vajra.

One takes as the object and contemplates the form of Dharma, which has the nature of a *vajra*—that is, of Akṣobhya. Upon that *yogapīṭha*, one [contemplates] that which is of a single nature (*ekasvabhāvām*). Because it is conjoined with the consort who is its own nature (*svābhavidyā*), it is both "one" (*ekā*) and "of the nature of itself" (*svabhāvā*); thus, it is "the form of Dharma," which, as before, refers to liberation. He explains that very nature of the *vajra*, the arising of the body of Vajrasattva, with the words beginning with "jaṭā": adorned with a crown of matted hair, and his color is blue by nature.

He meditates upon the excellent samādhi of Vajrasattva; this is that state of being (*bhāva*). The Blessed One is adorned with a crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmukuṭa*) resplendent with the five Buddhas, and his color is blue. In this way, one should meditate upon the perfect samādhi of Vajrasattva. "This one" refers to the yogi who, by virtue of co-existence, is "of the same nature" (*sabhāva*), meaning he is full of reverence. However, Akṣobhya’s crown of matted hair possesses the single external sign of a jewel, not the signs of the [other] Buddhas.

Now, does Akṣobhya also arise from the melting of the moon? No; he says "akka" and so forth. "Akka" is a syllabic foot (*gaṇa*) consisting of three morae (*mātrā*). "Majjaṭṭhiu" consists of five morae. One contemplates the arising of the syllable situated within the solar disc (*arka-maṇḍala*). Having brought forth the form of the syllable, one contemplates it as having the nature of a *vajra*. "Arka" means the sun; the "syllable" is the blue *hūṃ* syllable. However, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of Vajrasattva is the white *hūṃ* syllable. "Having the nature of a *vajra*" refers to the form of Akṣobhya.

He states that even the birth of the supreme being (*varasatva*) arises from mantra alone, beginning with the words "in water" (*jalatau*) and so forth. Here, the first group of syllables should be made four *mātrās* long by means of rapid pronunciation. The practitioner of mantra (*mantrī*) meditates upon his own form as the essential nature (*svabhāva*). He takes hold of Vajrasattva, whose essential nature is non-dual form. "Water" refers to the moon-fluid; it is the "end" (*anta*) of the principles (*tattva*) and of the parents. That which is born from that is the "form of oneself," meaning one’s own essential nature, the seed-syllable of one's own deity.

The mantra practitioner meditates on that moon-maṇḍala situated within [the heart], and by means of that seed-syllable, he meditates on Vajrasattva, whose intrinsic nature is the non-dual form. How is it the non-dual form? Because it appears as neither object nor cognition, or because of its union with one's own consort (svavidyā).

Applying the yoga, he states its fruit, beginning with "This," and so forth. This accomplishment of the mind (*cittaniṣpatti*) has been taught by Vajradhara; therein, by means of that state (*bhāva*), one meditates and thus accomplishes the intrinsic nature of the mind. The accomplishment of the mind is the yoga of the mind of Vajradhara. By means of that state—that is, by way of that mode—one meditates upon Vajrasattva, and he becomes accomplished as the intrinsic nature of the mind of Vajradhara.

If even for Vajradhara there is no arising from mantra—since it is impossible for one established in the non-conceptual *samādhi* to produce a body—then his emergence from that *samādhi* would be uninstigated; it would result in nothing but distraction or a state lacking a leader. Therefore, he says "ea" and so forth. Here, in each quarter-verse, there are four groups of four morae (*mātrā*). This single-natured Four-Goddess [mantra] manifests through song its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*) by means of space (*kha*).

In this way, one meditates on the goddess whose intrinsic nature is the mind established in the Dharma; that is to say, the fourfold goddess whose intrinsic nature is liberation. "Of a single nature" means having the form of liberation. "By song" refers to the four songs (*caturgītaka*) to be described below; "state" (*bhāva*) means intention (*abhiprāya*). "One makes her such" means one meditates upon her; the meaning is that one awakens her by generating the intention in the form of the mantra.

What does he awaken? [The syllable] *kha* means the essence (*sabhāva*), the state of equality (*samānabhāva*), that which is equal to space (*khasama*), and the fluidity of phenomena (*dharmadrava*). The word *ea* has this same meaning and must be understood from the vernacular (*prākṛta*), since even the vernacular enters into the Apabhraṃśa, as in examples such as *janto dvia dvia*.

This being so, the yogi meditates upon the fluidity of phenomena as having the nature of the mind, having assumed the form of Vajradhara, and also the form of the Goddess; for Vajrasattva is the perfectly pure mind whose nature is liberation, and the Goddess is perfectly pure Suchness (*tathatā*)—this is the intended meaning.

In order to provide himself as an example for the point that Buddhahood is attained through this very cultivation, a certain Buddha, having assembled his retinue, spoke even though the matter had not been explicitly requested: "Vajrasattva," and so forth. The lines of these two [stanzas] consist of three *gaṇas*; there is a doubling of the syllable *pīṭha-pa*, while there is no doubling of the syllable *utpatti-pa*. The term *upattiho* consists of four *mātrās* due to the combination of a short and a protracted [syllable].

I have seen Vajrasattva rejoicing in the yoga-seat (yogapīṭha), taking a consort and remaining in perfect equality, maintaining his attire; from his own nature, there is the arising from existence. Indeed, he who was seen there, Vajrasattva, plunges into and emanates the Buddhas, being firmly established.

“Wife” (*dārā*) means the consort; “entirely equal” (*sakalasamām*) means equal to the Blessed One in every respect. For just as the Blessed One is blue, with matted locks and a crown adorned by the five Buddhas, holding a crossed-vajra (*viśvavajra*) in his right hand and a bell marked with a crossed-vajra in his left, so too does this Blessed Lady stand. The word “who” (*yaḥ*) is to be supplied [as the subject]. “Adornment of dress” (*veṣaprasādhana*) is due to “the state of being equal” (*sabhāvāt*), that is, due to having an identical nature. “From the state of being” (*bhāvāt*) means from the existence of all sentient beings, which is to say, from the fluidity of the Dharma (*dharmadrava*).
“She plunges into” (*avagāhate*) means she discerns; “her” (*tām*) is to be supplied [as the object].

To the question "How so?", he says: "He expands," and so forth. "Established" means concentrated in mind. Regarding "Vajra" and so on: here, in the *ayuk* (odd) meters there are three *gaṇas*, while in the *yuk* (even) meters there are two; the word *jja* and the word *kha* signify the meaning. He who possesses the four natures is established in the midst of the four goddesses; he has entered the three worlds by way of the nature of *māyā*.

The infinite distinctions of body, speech, mind, and their respective activities for each of all the Buddhas are condensed into four secrets: the secret of body, the secret of mind, the secret of speech, and the secret of activity. Their suchness (*tathatā*) is, respectively, the four goddesses.

Therefore, they possess four natures; for this very reason, they are white, blue, red, and green, with Vajradharas of corresponding colors at their right sides. With their left hands, they hold a wheel, a red utpala, a lotus, and a blue utpala; their jeweled crowns are adorned by the Tathāgatas of their own respective families. Seated in their midst in the vajra-paryaṅka posture, he appears as a manifestation through their very nature of being like an illusion (*māyopama*). By them, the three worlds—the three secrets of the Tathāgata—are embraced, entered, and thoroughly penetrated as being like an illusion. They are thus discerned.

From here on, there are three *dvipadikā* meters, with four *gaṇas* per foot; however, the third consists of two feet. Regarding "viśvavajra" and so forth: *viśvavajra* refers to the four-faced [form] of the deity Vajradhara. "Therein" means within the moon at the heart. Even the Buddhas perform all manner of miraculous transformations (*vikurvaṇa*) for him, precisely because they are emanated from him. He states the utility of the emanated Buddhas: "In whatever way they arise. "Deva" means those who have become gods.
"Ho" is an address to the Buddhas. The remainder of the sense is: "Indeed, that is the attainment of all miraculous transformations."

"Let there be the miraculous transformation (*vikurvitam*) of Viśvavajra and of the Buddhas; what then of Vajrasattva? To this he says: *sabbau*, etc. "Of all the gods" means of the Buddhas and so forth; *āma* is the state of being (*umbhāva*). "Arising" (*jayantī*) refers to their manifestation through that [power]. *Vajjasattaho* is the state of the genitive case (*ḍaso bhāvaḥ*). *Tentati* means "all that. The sense is that everything is indeed the miraculous transformation of Vajrasattva alone; the meaning is that everything is produced by Vajrasattva himself in those various forms. And therefore: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmasvabhāva*) is seen everywhere; the three worlds are entirely of this very nature."

For Darva, Viśvavajra, and the others, this is indeed the Dharma. It is non-dual gnosis (*advayajñāna*) alone that is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and not an object nor a [dualistic] cognition, because of such discernment. For this very reason, the three worlds, the circle of Yoginīs, or the entire universe in its totality, is seen as having but a single intrinsic nature; thus it continues. "While playing," and so forth: while performing play, I saw the Buddha, and all his yogic powers (*yogaiśvarya*) were seen by me. "The gods," and so forth: the gods are Vajrasattva and the others; their *samaya* is the reality (*tattva*), and the chapter (*paṭala*) is that which illuminates it.

*Ādimuṃ* means *ādimaḥ*, the first; the suffix *ka* is used in the sense of the base word itself (*svārthe*), and there is an optional substitution of *uṃ* for its vowel. [The syllables] *āimauṃ*, *evaṃ*, *vidijjauṃ*, *taḍjauṃ*, *catusthauṃ*, and *paścamauṃ*.
This is the first chapter of the *Khasamatantra* within the *Khasamāyā*.

In some places the Goddess is recited as one, and in others as four goddesses. Therefore, in order to dispel doubt, the four goddesses ask about the number of goddesses with the words "Tell us" (*āikkha*) and so forth. Here, the odd [pādas] have six mātrās each, and the even [pādas] have ten mātrās each; *samaya* means the maṇḍala; the connection is "I shall explain the [number] of the goddesses. [The question is: "In your supreme *samaya*, how many goddesses are there? *Sauttama* means "O best of the ever-present ones" (*sadottama*); "supreme" (*uttama*) refers to the principal deity, and "ever-present" (*sada*) means that which is always joined (*saṃyukta*) within this [maṇḍala]. Thus, he is the "best of the ever-present ones" (*sadottama*).

The author of the commentary says: "Then," and so forth. This is a *trigaṇā* [verse consisting of three groups]; with one foot, the Blessed One speaks the *caturgītaka* in that location. Why? Because right here their names are specified. Furthermore, in the world, it is well known that when many things are mentioned, they are presented in an order beginning with the principal one. Thus, it is understood that Bhādevī is the principal one, and that the goddesses of Peace (*Śānti*) and the others reside respectively in the petals of the directions starting from the East, rather than being merely a list of numbers. "Suṇṇā iea" and so forth.

These four songs illustrate, respectively, the illusory nature of the secrets of mind, speech, and body. They serve to encourage the flow of the Dharma-fluid for the sake of embracing those very [secrets]. The meter used here is *pramitākṣarā*. In each foot of this meter, there are four groups (*gaṇa*) of four morae (*mātrā*). The first and third groups end with a long syllable; in the second, the long syllable occurs only in the middle.

Emptiness, non-discrimination, the created phenomena, equality, radiance, peace, liberation, supreme bliss, and inequality—[all these] are like illusions; they sport in their activity like Buddhas, equal to space, and peerless.

Because the mental aspects (*ākāra*) have ceased, it is "empty" (*śūnya*); and because no differentiation is perceived therein, it is "non-distinct" (*aviveka*). Thus, it is "empty and non-distinct" (*śūnyāviveka*). Because it has been produced according to the principle of the formation of space, and because it consists of the essence of all the fluid-like qualities of a Buddha, they address the Dharma itself with three epithets and urge the gods [to listen]. They say it is "equal" (*sama*), meaning it is identical to you because its nature is that very suchness (*tattathatā*). To the question "Which are these?", he says: "Light" (*bhā*) and so forth. It is called "being" (*bhāva*) because it does not shine in this way while remaining in the lap of the Lord (*pati*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that she shines intensely because she embodies the gathering of the four goddesses. She is *Śānti* (Peace) because she pacifies all physical afflictions; *Mokṣā* (Liberation) because she releases one from all mental obscurations; *Suśamā* (Excellent Peace) because she leads to the attainment of delight in all the qualities of a Buddha; and *Asamā* (Unequaled) because she accomplishes the welfare of the world through infinite emanations. If these five goddesses are equal, how then are they diverse in the forms of Bhāgavatī and the others? To this he says: "But [they are] *māyā*. Although they are equal, the word "but" (*tu*) has the sense of "however" (*māyā*). Thus, while they are essentially equal, they appear diverse through their illusory power.

Due to the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) by mantras and so forth, wood and other such materials appear in the form of elephants and the like—which are non-existent—and this is *māyā*. Because they share this same nature, the goddesses are also *māyā*. This is because within the vibration of the *dharmakāya*, which is pure mundane gnosis, they manifest in the form of various non-existent bodies, speech, and minds. To the question "For what reason are the goddesses *māyā*?", he says: "The effect is the reason, for the sake of the world's welfare. And therefore, they are equal to the Buddhas; that is, they are equal to the Buddhas such as Vajrasattva and others.

For they too, being identical with the *dharmakāya*, appear in the *saṃbhogakāya*—which has as its nature the pure mundane gnosis that is its outflow—in various forms for the sake of performing activities for the benefit of the world. To the question "What follows from this?", he says: "They sport," and so forth. All the goddesses, who are equal to space, and the Buddhas sport; having come together, they delight in the conduct for the sake of all beings. For how long? He says: "Incomparable" (*asamā*). Because "peace" (*śama*) means tranquility or destruction, and because they lack that, they are "non-peaceful" (*aśamā*); for it is said that the Tathāgatas possess eternal bodies.

For the Tathāgatas are eternal by way of all three bodies: by way of the essential body (*svābhāvikakāya*), because it is eternal by nature due to being without beginning or end; by way of the enjoyment body (*sāmbhogikakāya*), because it is eternal through aspiration due to its lack of termination; and by way of the emanation body (*nairmāṇikakāya*), because it is eternal through continuity, since even when one [emanation] perishes, that very same [body] arises elsewhere, while another remains in its place, like a mass of fire clinging to a great forest. Thus, this is an exhortation for the sake of embracing the playful mind whose nature is the enjoyment of the Dharma.

Because it accomplishes the welfare of the world, because it is pure, and because it is free from affliction, the six-syllable mantra is here the eternal *dhruvaka*. [The syllables are: *ru-lu-ru-lu-bhya-u-ru-ṭ*. "Illusion," and so forth.

Phenomena (*dharma*) have the nature of illusion; they shine like a lamp that has been lit. They are equal to those whose sound is the same, equal to phenomena, non-playful, equal to the sky, equal to those who do not meet, parts that are without conjunction, and naturally equal to a lute.

"Equal to space" refers to the Buddhas and goddesses whose nature is the *dharmakāya*. "Phenomena" (*dharmāḥ*) refers to the phenomena of the teaching; they are [equal] by means of those very [phenomena], and the meaning is that even they are equal to space because they appear as being equal to space.

For this very reason, they are "without play" (*akrīḍāḥ*), for those equal to space do not play; or rather, how could there be play for that which is equal to space? Because they appear through illusion (*māyā*) as having a common nature—that is, as having identical forms—due to such a determination (*pariccheda*). They have a "similar sound," meaning an echo (*pratiśabda*); the sounds consisting of that [echo] possess the property of similar sound, and they are "equal" because they are mere appearances. "Coming together" (*samāgama*) means a collection (*saṃghāta*); because that is absent, their parts—the phonemes (*varṇa*)—are "without coming together. These are the properties of the phonemes, because they are uttered in succession and because they perish as soon as they are uttered.

Furthermore, phonemes (*varṇa*) that are not combined are not expressive; nor are those that are not expressive [phonemes] factors of dharma (*dharma*). Therefore, dharmas are like space. For this very reason, they are by their own nature like a lute (*vīṇā*), meaning like the sound of a lute, because they are non-expressive sounds and because they lack intentionality. "Like the moon in water" (*kaajoasamā*): *kaṃ* means water, with the suffix *ka* used in its own sense (*svārthe*). Thus, the meaning is "like the moon in water. Alternatively, *dyota* means a lamp; they are equal to one who has produced light.

The meaning is that they have become the light of knowledge for a world fallen into the darkness of ignorance. Thus, by this [verse], their capacity to accomplish the welfare of the world is proclaimed; by the remainder [of the verse], their purity is shown. Therefore, the collective sense is: "You too, having emerged, teach the Dharmas. Regarding the passage beginning with *jo* (yo):
"That light of Dharma which is equal to space—upon that, the Vajras act, being equal to form.
It is like the ocean and the Lord of the Gods, possessing much [virtue] through the inexhaustible bliss of unchanging form; upon that, the Vajra is supreme."

The very Dharma of all the Buddhas has become equalized (*samarasībhūta*); it is illumination because its nature is luminosity, and it is equal to space because it is free from appearance (*nirābhāsa*). Having manifested within that, the Vajras and Vajrasattvas perform transformations and display the Dharmas for the benefit of sentient beings. One might ask: "Are they of the nature of form? To which he replies: "Equal to form. This is because they distinguish themselves by being mere appearances of form. The system (*naya*) of those Vajras is the mandala. As to what kind it is, he says: "From form," and so forth.

The five objects of desire are form and so forth; because he bestows inexhaustible bliss through them, he is described as such. "The ocean" refers to rivers, ponds, and the like. "In this [ocean], Indra" refers to the moon; he is equal to it by virtue of being delimited as a reflection. Thus, all Buddhas, who are equal to space, manifest bodies and the maṇḍalas of embodied beings for the sake of sentient beings. Therefore, the intention is: "You too should manifest both. "Abundant," and so forth.

Therein, the Vajra Way possesses many seats of yoga (*yogapīṭha*) and assumes many forms; therein, he who consists of vajra emanates sentient beings as equal to himself; therein, the Vajra grants boons equal to the [three] elements. He is so called because he has many seats of yoga. Because of his being that within them, he is "consisting of vajra," "vajra-natured," and "Vajradhara"; he sustains [beings] according to the differences in the dispositions of those to be trained.

In that very place, he emanates [beings] through the differentiation of forms; from that very source, he makes sentient beings equal to himself as Buddhas and so forth by virtue of his power, because they are its vibration. Thus, "by those beings" refers to Vajra, the Holder of the Vajra (*vajradhara*). He "bestows a body," meaning he grants the desired boons such as Buddhahood and so forth. "Equal to the elements" (*dhātusama*) means equal to the lineage (*gotrasama*), which is to say, according to one's lineage. As for the reading *jei* found in some versions, it means "he conquers" and "he disciplines"; the sense there is that he disciplines the excellent elements—the three-thousandfold world systems—at a time equal to all.

The sense is: "O Vajradhara, carry out such activity for the benefit of others. Having thus taught the four songs (*caturgītaka*) to the four goddesses so that they might know their respective numbers and so forth, he says "e" and so on in order to enjoin them. In these [songs], there are four groups (*gaṇa*) of four morae (*mātrā*) per line; the shortening in "āṇei vajja" is for the sake of filling the meter.

These four goddesses have uttered this song. One who is established in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that is equal to space (*khasama*), and who exhorts the Lord, hears this song and perceives it through the body of sound. With a single-pointed mind—that is, with a concentrated mind—one penetrates his own mind through the mantra-repetition (*japa*) by means of the body of meaning. To the question "What then?", he says: "Come here" (*eha*), and so forth. This song is equal to space because it is a manifestation of suchness (*tathatā*).

He brings forth the Vajradhara who is identical in form [to himself]; for that purpose, he awakens the mind—which consists of the essence of the Dharma-fluid made of vajra—and causes it to emerge; by means of a single nature, he brings the continuum of the Vajra-way to fruition.

Now, regarding the arising of Vajra and the Vajra-method, he asks: "Which are the mantras? and says: *vajrapadena*, etc. In this [verse], there are three groups (*gaṇa*) of four morae (*mātrā*) per line. The "Vajra-word" (*vajrapada*) is the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the Vajra-holder, namely the syllable *hūṃ*. By that, the seed-syllable is distinguished from other natures. The connection is: "one meditates upon [the deity] from a single seed, which is the fluid of Dharma (*dharmadrava*). The meaning is: "by means of that very fluid of Dharma, one meditates upon the five *hūṃ*s. To the question "What is done by that?", he says: *cet ta*, etc.

The mind is the holder of the blue vajra; that maṇḍala in which he resides is what one meditates upon as a whole. For in the Apabhraṃśa language, the word *sarva* has three forms; when the letter *r* is elided, there is an option for the dual number. In the absence of the dual, there is either the lengthening of the preceding vowel *a* or the substitution of *ha* for *va*. [As for the question] "How is the meditation on the five seed-syllables performed from the fluid of Dharma?", he says: "Dhamma," and so forth. This is an *anuṣṭubh* meter called *pathyāvaktra*, and in this case: "In the feet, after the first [syllable], there shall not be two light syllables together."
The *y* of both the odd and even [pādas], however, occurs after the fourth syllable when followed by *jas*.

The mandala is the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*); that which stands in its center is the supreme lotus, and the meditation upon that is said to be the meditation upon the Dharma. "The supreme meditation on the lotus of the pure Dharma-mandala"—this refers to the mind of that [Dharma]. The remainder of the sense is that one meditates upon the differentiator of that Dharma as the mind. This occurs because within the pericarp and the petals of the directions, that Dharma undergoes transformation into the form of the syllable *HŪṂ* mounted upon a moon. To the question of what one should do after that, he says: "MĀA," and so forth.

In each quarter of these two [verses], three groups (gaṇas) perform the investigation of all form, which indeed has the nature of illusion; this is the ellipsis. O [you], contemplate the single nature of the mind, whose nature is the vajra—the Vajra-way.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the mind is the Vajra-method (*vajranaya*), and not that it is an illusion (*māyā*)? [Response] To this, he says "O, mind! and so forth. Because mental forms (*ākāra*) lack reality due to being devoid of a nature that is either one or many, the mind is of the same nature as space (*khena sarūpam*). Its method, the Mind-method (*cittanaya*), is without intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*). The meaning is that the Mind-method of the Vajra-method is, by virtue of the mind's own nature, without intrinsic nature; it is "without form" (*asvarūpa*), which means it is false (*mithyā*).

One might object: "Is not the *vajra* one thing and the *vajranaya* another, given the difference in their appearances? How then can they have a single nature? To this he says, "Both," and so forth. There is no method (*naya*)—that is, no logical principle—for that which possesses a manifold nature, because in that which is like space, mere luminosity, the mental forms (*ākāra*) are unreal. When that state of abiding exists, the *vajra* itself—and thus the *Vajradhara* who is like space—is the very nature; everything else is illusion, due to its unreality. Regarding "the essence of the *vajra*" (*vajrasattva*), and so forth: in each quarter-verse (*pratipāda*), there are four metrical feet (*gaṇa*), each consisting of four morae (*mātrā*).

By the first [verse], he states that my form is artificial; by the second, that the secret of mind and speech is the state of the Hevajra-sattva, which is of a single nature (*ekasvabhāva*). The remainder is: "The sign of the world is created by you, whose nature is illusion (*māyāsvabhāva*). To the question "How so?", he says: "O Sattva," and so forth. That by which beings are disciplined is *vinaya*, a distinction of form. One whose nature is discipline awakens beings. The state of being the Hevajra-sattva is precisely the natural state (*prakṛti*) of the single nature. *Devī* means "O Goddess."

*Vollai* means he speaks; *vajja* refers to Vajradhara; *aḍeguha* means hidden or secret, which signifies the secret of mind and speech. *Abbhantare* means within one's own heart; *ramanta uṃ* means rejoicing. By way of the nature of the mind, in the form of a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) situated upon a moon-mandala, *tahija* means indeed in the heart; *cittanigūḍha* means concealed within the hub (*varaṭaka*) of the double-vajra. *Dhammai siddhauṃ*—thus the mantra is also emanated, and that is the syllable *HŪṂ*. Regarding the radiation [of light], he says "sphāra" and so forth.
For the odd [syllables] there are eight morae (*mātrā*), and for the even [syllables] twelve.
In the other [direction], there are fourteen for the odd-numbered years and twelve for the even-numbered years.

The mantra of the Vajra-heart expands sentient beings, who are of the nature of space and like an illusion. It then withdraws them again, because the nature of mind is one. For when all things are examined by the mind, I see everything as equal and identical in its illusory nature; thus, I repeatedly bring together and withdraw sentient beings, making them of a single form.

By all of this, the following is stated: here, preceded by the sevenfold unsurpassed worship, taking refuge, and the generation of the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*), one should resolve upon the state of mind-only (*cittamātratā*); having brought the thought of awakening, which is equal to space, before oneself, one should consecrate it with: *oṃ śūnyatājñānavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham* ("I am of the nature of the vajra of the wisdom of emptiness").

Thereafter, having visualized the goddess Cundā, born from the syllable *cuṭ*, white as the moon, four-armed, with one hand in the gesture of meditative equipoise (*samādhimudrā*) holding an alms-bowl and the other two hands holding a rosary and a book, wearing a crown of matted locks, seated in the vajra-paryaṅka posture upon the moon of a great lotus, and equal in size to the world-system; and within the pericarp of that lotus, which is as clear and white as a pearl and assumes the form of the source of phenomena (*dharmodayā*), there is a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) produced from the transformation of the syllable *bhrūṃ* and Vairocana, consisting of five most radiant jewels, square, with four doors and adorned with four archways.
And in the four goddesses, he saw a host of beautiful Apsarases engaged in the foremost of worship.
Adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, silk bands, garlands, chowries, and other ornaments,
it resounded with the bells and the tops of its banners fluttering in the wind.

Having meditated thus, one should visualize an eight-petaled red lotus in its center; upon the solar disc at its pericarp, by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*, one should contemplate the Blessed Lord Akṣobhya, resembling a sapphire, wearing a crown of matted hair marked with a jewel, slightly wrathful with bared fangs, adorned with variegated garments and ornaments, and embracing with both arms his own consort who holds a vajra and a vajra-bell. Having summoned [the Tathāgatas] from all directions by the sound of illusory amorous play and caused them to enter through the mouth, they dissolve into the Tathāgata and pass into the interior of the lotus.

One should contemplate [the lotus] as consisting of great bliss (*mahāsukha*). Beholding one's mother and father dissolved by its radiance, one should see that lotus filled with the moon-melting essence, which is the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas. Thereupon, the four goddesses—Śānti, Mokṣā, Suṣamā, and Asamā—seated upon the moons at the four gates, should exhort Mahāvajradhara, who is of the nature of the *dharmakāya*, for the sake of rousing him from that non-conceptual samādhi of the great bliss of liberation, by means of a fourfold song:
"Empty is this world, equal to the Dharma; they proclaim liberation, peerless and sublime."
They show compassion like illusions; they sport like Buddhas, equal to all that is empty, peerless.
They speak with a nature like illusion, unborn and peerless, their speech being equal to the Dharma.
Phenomena are without play, equal to the empty, peerless, and without meeting—this is like the lute.
One should avoid those worldly dharmas which create expectations;

therein, one should avoid that which resembles form (rūpa), because it is unshakable by the pleasure of desires such as form, like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. One should avoid that which is the seat of the three-fold suffering; one should avoid that which assumes many forms. 3.1–2.1.
"They pierce the seven [syllables] equal to the noseless [A], and there they place the Vajra equal to the excellent metal [HŪM].

(4) Having thus sung these verses, the four goddesses enter and dissolve into the liquids in the petals of their respective directions and become of one flavor (*samarasī*). Furthermore, in accordance with the verses, by means of that lunar liquid, there should be five *hūṃ*-syllables on moon-seats in the petals starting from the east at the pericarp.

One should visualize a universal vajra (*viśvavajra*) upon the *karṇikā* [of the lotus] by means of the syllable *HŪṂ*, which is blue, white, dark blue, red, and green respectively; and from the *HŪṂ*s in the east and other directions, one should visualize five-pronged vajras of corresponding colors. Through the radiation of rays from the seed-syllables produced within the central hub (*varaṭaka*), one performs acts for the benefit of the world, and those vajras transform accordingly into the forms of the six deities. Among them, the transformation of the seed-syllable of the universal vajra is the Blessed Lord Vajrasattva.

Resembling a sapphire, wearing a crown of matted hair, in the prime of youth, and adorned with variegated garments and ornaments, he sits in the vajraparyaṅka posture. Embracing his own consort with both hands—which hold a double-vajra (viśvavajra) marked by a double-vajra on its top—he abides as the hero embodying the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgārarasa).

On the eastern petal is Śānti, white in color, arisen from the seed-syllable of a white vajra; on the southern petal is Mokṣā, blue in color, arisen from the seed-syllable of a blue vajra; on the western petal is Suṣamā, the color of a ruby, arisen from the seed-syllable of a red vajra; and on the northern petal is Asamā, the color of emerald, arisen from the seed-syllable of a green vajra.

These four [consorts], in the bloom of youth, embodying the sentiments of erotic love (*śṛṅgāra*) and heroism (*vīra*), wearing jeweled crowns and various garments and ornaments, gaze at the Blessed One with smiling sidelong glances. With their right hands they hold five-pronged vajras of the same color as themselves, and with their left hands they hold a wheel, a red lotus, a lotus, and a blue lotus respectively; they sit upon the being in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).

Thereafter, having beheld a blue syllable *hūṃ*, garlanded with rays of light, within the moon at the center of the double-vajra (*viśvavajra*) between the breasts of the Blessed One and the Goddess Bhā, one should consecrate oneself with the thought: "I am of the nature of the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*)."

Having visualized the syllables *praṇava* (oṃ), *ākara* (hūṃ), and *hūṃ*—white, red, and black respectively—at the moon [disks] of the head, throat, and heart, one should empower them with the mantras: *oṃ sarvatathāgatakāyavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*, *oṃ sarvatathāgatavāgvajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*, *oṃ sarvatathāgatacittavajrasvabhāvātmako ’ham*.

One should visualize one's own seed-syllables within the moons located at the centers of the five-pronged vajras—which are the same color [as their respective deities]—situated upon the moons between the breasts of the four goddesses; and one should likewise visualize the *praṇava* (oṃ) and other syllables upon the moons at the head, throat, and heart. Then, having ascertained that the body, speech, and mind of all the deities are, according to reality, equal to space, formless because they lack substantiality, unarisen, and devoid of intrinsic nature, one should consecrate them with this verse:

"The syllable of the body is unarisen; it is characterized by the words of speech and mind. It is the non-conceptualization of the space-vajra, the gathering of what is falsely gathered. (Guhyasamāja 17.36)
Thus it is said.

Then, having summoned the *jñānamaṇḍala* by means of the radiance of one's own seed-syllables (*bīja*) emanating toward the ten directions, and having established it in the space before oneself, one should offer the water for honor (*argha*) recited from one's own heart. Having drawn in the *jñānamaṇḍala* with the syllables *aḥ hūṃ va hoḥ*, and having caused its entry, bound it, and brought it under control, one should visualize the *samayamaṇḍala* as having become one with it.

Then, having resolved that one is being consecrated—both oneself and the mandala—by Tathāgatas drawn forth by the rays of the heart-mantra who hold precious vases filled with the water of primordial wisdom, one should visualize the Family Tathāgatas within the crowns of the deities produced from that water.

Above the crown of matted hair on his own head, he visualizes the Blessed One Akṣobhya, resembling sapphire, standing in the earth-touching gesture (*bhūsparśamudrā*); above his forehead, Vairocana, resembling moonlight, standing in the gesture of supreme enlightenment (*bodhyagrīmudrā*); above his right ear, Ratnasambhava, golden in color, standing in the gesture of granting boons (*varadamudrā*); above the back of his neck, Amitābha, resembling a ruby, standing in the gesture of meditative concentration (*samādhimudrā*); and above his left ear, Amoghasiddhi, with the luster of emerald, standing in the gesture of fearlessness (*abhayamudrā*).

One should contemplate as follows: upon the jewel crowns of the four goddesses of Bhā-devī, one should visualize Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Amitāyus, and Amoghasiddhi in their respective order. Then, with the goddesses emanating from the rays of light issuing from the heart-mantra, pervading the expanse of the sky through the yoga of radiation, one should worship the Blessed One together with his retinue. Thereafter, having performed the domestic worship and the worship of the five essences according to the ritual rules, one should consecrate [the visualization] with: "Oṃ, I am of the nature of the vajra-worship of all Tathāgatas. Then, one should praise the Blessed One through the mouths of the four goddesses with three verses.
He who is the essence of the three worlds is the crown-jewel of the five Buddhas; his nature is the primordial state of Buddhahood, which is as boundless as space.
He who is the crown-jewel of the five Buddhas is the very nature of Dharma.
The twenty-fifth chapter on Vajrasattva, the majesty of the Dharma of the three worlds.
(1) Even through the end of the Vajrasattva mantra, merit becomes infinite.
Through the Vajrasattva vidyā, the great Dharma is attained. (2–3)

Thereafter, one should meditate upon oneself and the maṇḍala as being endowed with supreme bliss for as long as desired. Then, having emanated all the Tathāgatas from the rays issuing from the mouth of the heart-mantra and having made the world consist of them, one should contemplate the mind’s nature as the manifold form (*viśvarūpatā*). Having again withdrawn them, one should perceive the mind’s nature as a single essence (*ekasvabhāvatā*). In this tantra, the conventional practice of the three samādhis does not exist; here there is only a single samādhi called the Sovereign King of the Maṇḍala (*maṇḍalarājāgrī*). When weary from meditation, one should recite the mantra.

I cause the heart-mantra *hūṃ*, which resides within the hub of the universal vajra, to be impassioned; or the near-heart-mantra, or both, to be impassioned, *hūṃ*; or the seventeen-syllable mantra *oṃ mahāsukhavajrasattvajaḥ hūṃ vaṃ hoḥ suratas tvam*; or another appropriate mantra, vidyā, and so forth, one should recite. Then, one should make aspirational prayers. In brief, however, by means of two verses:
"By these roots of virtue, may I attain the state of the Holder of the Great Vajra, the all-in-all of all Buddhas; and may that entire world attain it. (1)
"The conduct for the sake of awakening, and furthermore that which was described by Bodhivajra for the Fully Awakened Ones— that conduct of mine is indeed twofold. Then,

having dissolved the pledge-maṇḍala drawn in by the rays of light from the mantra together with the assembly, and having arisen therefrom, one should dwell at ease within oneself through the *phaṭ*-syllable of one's own deity, by means of the meditative resolve (*adhimokṣa*) upon the four goddesses in the four elements.

This is the procedure for the first twilight session (*prathamasandhyā*). However, during the other twilights, one should instantly take as one's object of focus oneself in the form of the deity together with the *vidyā*, fully perfected. Then, having sequentially emitted the four goddesses from the mantra at one’s own heart and established them in their respective places, one should perform everything—the empowerment of the body (*kāyādhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth—as before.

Thus, at the evening twilight, having worshipped the Knowledge Maṇḍala and offered the water of honor (*arghya*), one should dismiss it with the mantra *oṃ vajramūrti* and perform self-protection. One should then internalize the Samaya Maṇḍala within one's own mantra. At the time of sleep, one should fall asleep having brought face-to-face the infinite, non-manifesting gnosis (*jñāna*). Awakened from sleep by the four goddesses through the four songs of exhortation, one should act in this manner at each [twilight] until one perceives the signs of accomplishment (*siddhi*).
This is the Mind-Predominant Maṇḍala, the Mind Maṇḍala; the chapter that elucidates it is the [eighth] chapter.
In the *Khasamā*, the commentary on the *Khasamatantra*, this is the second chapter, the Chapter on the Mind Maṇḍala.

The mandala of speech (*vāṅmaṇḍala*) must be explained. Speech is wisdom (*prajñā*), mind is method (*upāya*); the non-dual state of wisdom and method is the mandala of speech, and that is primarily based upon wisdom. Therefore, in order to introduce its goddess, he says "dia" and so forth. Here, in each foot of the three *dvipadikā* meters, there are four groups (*gaṇa*) of four morae (*mātrā*). The twice-born are the Brahmins, and they are of the same nature as the *caṇḍālas* because both are merely consciousness (*vijñānamātra*), and because the characteristics that differentiate them lack any real existence.
By this illustration, the Buddha has explained that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and primordial essence (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena is mere luminosity, equal to space.

[Objection: Is it not the case that even though entities possess multiple intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), these are established by appearance; and even a single nature is impossible for that which is not of the nature of luminosity (*aprakāśātman*) because it would lack appearance? So how can unity be proclaimed rather than multiplicity? [The author] says: "One" (*eka*), and so forth. The state of being mind-only (*cittamātratā*) is its established existence as a single intrinsic nature, because that is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); it is not multiple, because multiplicity is merely imagined (*kalpita*). When that [single nature] exists, the Vajrin (the Holder of the Vajra) speaks of an identical nature. He states another example with the words beginning "O Brāhmaṇa," and so forth.

The Brahmin and the dog are of one and the same nature, because both the bone and the ornament—such as bracelets and earrings—are illusory in nature. *Vajjapaaṃ* means that which is to be performed with delay; the "vajra-word" (*vajrapada*) is the firm form, which is mind-only (*cittamātratā*). Within that [state], such as the Brahmin and the dog, there is truth, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Now, he asks: by whom has this identical nature therein been seen? He says: *mai jo iā*, "it was seen by me. He states another example, beginning with *mutta*.

"Devīṃ bhādevīṃ tahiṃ" (the goddesses, by their nature, there)—in that state of single-nature (*ekasvabhāvatā*), "joa" (yoga) means *sabhāveti* (by nature); this is to be supplied with a slow [recitation]. Yoga is meditative absorption (*samādhi*). "Tahiṃ" means in that yoga. "Sabb tumha" means all of you, the four goddesses; this is the meaning. Being of a single nature with Bhāva, who is Vajrasattva, they shine forth. "Prabhāvyate" means it is manifested or displayed; thus it is *prabhāva*. "Śarīraṃ" means having a single body (*ekaśarīrā*); this is the meaning. "Tulla" and so forth...

In each quarter-verse of this [stanza], there are fourteen mātrās. Because they share the same nature due to being half-fluid (*ardhadravatva*), he is "single-minded" (*ekamanā*) and "single-mantra" (*ekamantra*). "Vajra should awaken; Vajrasattva should awaken"—he is a single person, existing alone. If one asks, "Where have the mother and father gone?", he says: "There," and so forth. In that *dharmadrava* (the fluid of Dharma), the two—the nature of hatred and its own-being—Akṣobhya and his consort, have perished. "By the half-limb" means by the half-body; this is the manifestation (*prabhāvanā*) of the power of Dharma, which is Vajrasattva.

Some read the verse as follows: *addhe aṅge*. For them, the fourth quarter would consist of sixteen mātrās. He asks what the other half is: *vajjadāru*, etc. In each quarter of these two [lines], there are three groups (*gaṇa*) of four mātrās each. *Vajjaho* consists of four mātrās due to its short vowel, while *gaṇa* consists of three mātrās due to its slow (*vilambita*) pronunciation.

"Vajradārā" means the wife of Vajra, namely Bhagavati. She is bestowed upon the Yogin during that propagation of the Dharma by Vajra—that is, by the Holder of the Vajra—as one who is of a single nature and a single body, because she fills his left half as his very own consort (*svābhā*). When does her arising occur? To this he says: "vajjaho," and so forth. As long as the description and praise of Vajra—the fluid of Dharma—is being performed through the four songs of the four goddesses with the sound *ruṇaruṇāya*, for that long [she arises].

Immediately after that, [the question] "What is the power of the Dharma? follows. Furthermore, regarding where the fourfold assembly of deities goes, he says "devaho" and so forth. The meaning is that one should see them as unified with the portion of the Goddess from the left side of the deity Vajrasattva.

[Objection: "Is it not the case that Vajrasattva is to be meditated upon by us, whereas this [deity] is something else entirely, being neither female nor male? To this, he says "Vajrasattva," and so forth. The meaning is: let this very Vajrasattva be prostrated to and meditated upon; let my word be accepted as authoritative, because I too am that very Blessed One.

This is what is meant: having brought face-to-face the *bodhicitta* equal to space (*khasama*) through the sequence of the sevenfold supreme worship and so forth, one should visualize the Blessed Lady Cundā with a body three thousand worlds in size by means of the syllable *Oṃ*. Then, having meditated upon a peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) produced from the transformation of Vairocana within the pericarp of her lotus, and having visualized the Blessed Lord Akṣobhya in its center—upon a solar disc in the pericarp of a red eight-petaled lotus—in union with his consort, one should cause all the Buddhas to enter and dissolve into him within the interior of the lotus.

Having observed that very place, one sees that wisdom and means have dissolved and become of one flavor (*samarasībhūta*). Then, having visualized the seed-syllable within the central hub of a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*)—which has arisen from the middle of a moon-maṇḍala produced by the withdrawal of the flow of Dharma prompted by the four songs of the four goddesses—one contemplates the transformation of that [seed-syllable] into the Blessed One. He bears the form of a male with his right half and the form of the goddess Bhā with his left half; he resembles a ruby (*padmarāga*), possesses a horse’s udder on the left, and on the left half of his forehead is adorned with locks of hair, wearing a crown of matted locks (*jaṭāmukuṭin*).

Having visualized [the central deity] with variegated ornaments and garments, and embodying the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*), one should contemplate the four goddesses entering that very left half and becoming of a single flavor (*ekarasa*). The remainder—the crown of the five Buddhas and so forth—is as before, according to the appropriate application. Thus has been described the chapter illuminating the mandala of speech.
This is the third chapter on the mandala of speech in the commentary on the *Khasamata* tantra, titled *Khasamā*.

The body maṇḍala is to be explained. In that regard, the supreme commitment (samaya) regarding the nourishment of the body by means of the body is stated as "elephant" (*hatthi*) and so forth. In these two [verses], there are four groups (*gaṇa*) in each quarter-verse whose intrinsic nature is equal to space; thus, one is possessed of the yoga of Vajrasattva. "O yogin" (*joi*); "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) together with the mind means a one-pointed mind, a single-mindedness. Through that single-mindedness toward the Holder of the Vajra (*vajradhara*), one attains accomplishment.

*rūpe svāṇa* means "having the form of Vajrasattva. There is a variant reading, *rūvasamāṇa*, which means "by way of similarity of form"; that is the meaning there. Now, he speaks of suchness (*tathatā*) by means of four verses of the goddess Śānti, because she has suchness as her intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Each of these [verses] consists of three metrical groups (*gaṇas*) per line. *Kuṇantau* means "of those performing"; *ea* means "thus," as he will explain. *Dhammasamā* means "phenomena (*dharmas*) are equal. *Samīau* means "let them be brought together" or "let them be correctly known"; although the referent is plural, the singular is used.
"Vāra" means "thus"; such deliberation is certainty. This deity is Vajrasattva, Vairocana, the Eternal; the goddesses are five. These possess a single nature.

One might object: "Should he not be called Akṣobhya rather than Vairocana? To this he says, "tulya" and so forth. For the yogin of equanimous mind, the *dharmakāya*—which is of a single flavor—is accomplished. Therefore, the manifestation here does not arise from Akṣobhya, who is characterized by non-agitation (*satva*), but rather from Vairocana, because he illuminates equality by shattering established constraints. Now, what is the benefit in arising from Vairocana? To explain the withdrawal of the reality of the body-maṇḍala, he says, "vajrasattva" and so forth. All these are to be contemplated as having a single intrinsic nature.

How is this so? As before, within the *kūṭāgāra* produced from Vairocana, which rests upon the pericarp of the Cundā-lotus, there is a lotus serving as the central seat; therein, through the fluid born of the union of Vairocana and his consort (*svābhā*), the two of them dissolve. Having arisen after the dissolution of the four goddesses, one meditates on the white Vajradhara, born from a white *hūṃ* syllable upon a moon disc produced from the solidification of that fluid. This arises from the *dharmakāya*, which is of a single nature. The "Vajra Way" (*vajranaya*) is the Vajrayāna. To the question, "What then is the meaning of *yogapīṭha*? he says: "Cundā," and so forth.

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and primordial essence (*prakṛti*) of all phenomena (*bhāva*, *sarvadharma*), which is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), is Cundā. Regarding what Vajrasattva does therein, it is said: "In that seat of yoga (*yogapīṭha*), being embodied and possessing a body, he perceives the single intrinsic nature of all phenomena. "Bhāvaṇa" means cultivation (*bhāvanā*); [this refers to] the eternal Vairocana. "Deviho" means the truth of the goddess, the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the Vajrin; his "origination" (*utpatti*) is indeed by way of the body. And since the body is eternal, he alone teaches that very origination.

To explain how this is so, he says: *essasī*, etc. Here, there are two *dvipadikās*; the odd [syllables] consist of fourteen *mātrās* each, while the even ones consist of twelve *mātrās*. *E* refers to the yogin who, with a one-pointed mind, visualizes the seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the mantra of the Vajra—the Vajradhara—namely the white syllable *HŪṂ*, situated in the center of the moon disc born from the withdrawal of the essence of phenomena (*dharmadrava*), as described by *sasimaṇḍalamajjhaṭiṭau*. By means of that mantra, there are three [prongs], meaning a twelve-pronged [vajra] with three prongs on each side.

Regarding "jalantauṃ," there is a reading "jvalat kavacit" (blazing and armored). "Cittai vajjasahāva vajjavibhāvai eamaṇā tisṛi vajrajalantaü" means that the mind has the nature of the vajra, the manifestations of the vajra, and is thus-minded; even there, the meaning is the same. However, [if one reads] "tisṛi" with a short vowel, it would not be a four-moraic *yamaka* [rhyme]. In "majjaṭṭiaüṃ," the suffix *-ka-* is added in its own sense (*svārthe*) to the middle element. Regarding "vajjasahāva"—it refers to the form of Vajradhara. "Emmai" means "thus by me"; the Vajra-method is the arising of Vajradhara. "Dhamauṃ" means "of phenomena" (*dharmāṇām*). This concludes the fourth chapter on the Body Maṇḍala in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) on the *Khasamata-tantra*.

One might ask: "Let the deity arise from the *dharmakāya* itself; what is the need for a mantra? To this he says: "In the absence," and so forth. Here, three [syllables] consist of two paths (*dvipatha*), and the fourth consists of three groups (*trigaṇa*). "In the absence" (*abhāve*) has four morae (*caturmātra*) due to its rapid pronunciation. "Absence" (*abhāva*) is non-conceptual meditative absorption (*samādhi*); "existence" (*bhāva*) is the body. It is not "cultivated" (*bhāvyate*) nor "uttered" (*jalpyate*). For even upon waking from a dream, one does not run toward a conceptualization that is truly unarisen. Likewise, even from the *dharmakāya*, there is no arising of the body without a mantra.

*Ammahō* is an address to a woman; *bhāvayati* means "he contemplates" or "he determines," thus *bhāva* is the mantra. *Ea* means "by this mantra. *Dhammanirūvajjau* means when the Dharma is being determined, [it arises] from the mind—that is, from the non-conceptual state designated as the mantra. He states another argument with the words: "The *bhāva* is the body; it is the manifestation of the light of consciousness (*cittahobhāsa*)," and so forth. From the mind alone, which is free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), there is no method (*naya*) or liberation (*mokṣa*) regarding the existence of the body; for that reason, the *bhāva* is made into the mantra.

To the question "Why does it not exist?", he says "existence" (*bhāva*) and so forth: there is no method (*naya*), that is, liberation, for the mind whose nature is that [of existence], because of their contradiction. What kind of method is it? It is the nature of the mind which is equal to space (*khasama*), due to the complete exhaustion of the representations (*vijñapti*)—which manifest as the support, the body, and objects—along with their seeds. This occurs through the power of the accumulations (*saṃbhāra*). If it is argued that "that same embodied being will come into existence again," he says "mind" (*citta*) and so forth: the mind of one who is being liberated becomes especially pure; it is exhausted such that there is no returning again.

What was that "prior tongue" (*pubbajiha*)? It was previously stated that there was first delusion (*bhrānti*), which is the appearance of the cause of delusion (*bhrāntinimitta*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "How," and so forth. How can the state of that body and so on—which has been exhausted through non-return—be brought about? Certainly not, because of contradiction. [Objection: In that case, let the very nature (*prakṛti*) of the mind be its form. Therefore, even a purified mind will arise in the form of a body. To this, he replies: "Is accomplished" (*sijjha*), and so forth.

And this is not a real entity, nor is it the body; thus, the system of ultimate reality—whether external or consisting of the nature of mind—is not established, because it is devoid of a nature that is either one or many. Consequently, the mind is indeed of the nature of space, since mental forms are insubstantial; and false appearance is delusion.

Furthermore, since there is no delusion (*bhrānti*) in the liberated mind, how could there be a body for it? Therefore, from that fluid *dharmakāya*, a consciousness which is its very outflow (*niṣyanda*) arises as the appearance of a body and so forth, for those who discern their own forms as unreal and themselves as being like an illusion (*māyopama*). This is the intended meaning. Concluding, he says: *majjha* and so on. The suffix *-ka* is used in the sense of the base word itself; thus, from the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*) arises conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and from that, the body.

By this method, in the middle of the *anuloma* sequence, the seed-syllable (*bījākṣara*) is the defining term. Thus, from the non-conceptual mind (*citta*) permeated by the mantra, the entity—the body—is produced. In this way, Vajrasattva arises with various natures such as the mind-mandala (*cittamaṇḍala*) and so forth. It has been said: "That which is cultivated through the perfection of all beings is made into the nature of liberation. And that liberation is mind-only (*cittamātra*), a single flavor (*ekarasa*). To the question of what kind of entity that is to be meditated upon (*bhāvya*), he says: "Acchauṃ," and so forth. In each quarter-verse (*pratipāda*) of this [stanza], there are three metrical groups (*gaṇas*).

"Clear" (*accha*) because of its natural purity; "stainless" (*nirmala*) because adventitious stains have been eliminated. Due to its similarity to water, the term "water" (*pānīya*) is used, meaning it flows easily with pleasure. "In that" (*tetthaho*) means by means of the generation of Vajrasattva. "Cultivating swift accomplishment" (*laghusīdhyam bhāvantam*) means by that state, by that which has been embodied. "This" (*emmai*) means consisting of this. "Told" (*kahi*) means it was spoken; it is unutterable (*anirutta*), yet it has been told. The suffix *kta* is used here in the sense of the action (*bhāve*). It is called "unuttered" (*nirūktam*) because it has emerged from what is expressed (*uktāt*).
