By the words "The secret of the vajra is unspeakable," and so forth, he states the *samaya*. In this [verse], the feet consist of four *gaṇas*; in "some" (*some*), the vowel *e* is short. In "āhāre" (*āhāre*), there is a short vowel at the beginning; "somena" (*somena*) means by means of the *bodhicitta*; "bhāva" (*bhāva*) means one's own body. "Tahiṃ" (*tahiṃ*) means when that exists; "vajrodaka" (*vajrodaka*) means liquor. "Evamsvabhāvam" (*evamsvabhāvam*) means having the nature of *bodhicitta*. "Cittasahāva" (*cittasahāva*) means abiding in the yoga of Vajrasattva. Regarding "dhamma" (*dhamma*) and so forth: the feet of these two [verses] consist of three *gaṇas*.

Dharma, Saṅgha, and Vajrodaka—these have the same essential nature (*tulyasvabhāva*). For Vajrodaka is indeed the *bodhicitta*; that itself is Dharma because it is the Noble Path (*āryamārga*), and that itself is the Saṅgha because it comprises individuals endowed with vigor (*savīryapudgala*). Furthermore, the common nature of the *vasā* (fats) and so forth is precisely the *bodhicitta*, because phenomena (*dharmas*) are mere appearances and their forms (*ākāras*) are unreal; thus, the state (*bhāva*) is transformed by the yogins through practice (*abhyāsa*) or intention (*āśaya*)—this is the remainder [of the sense]. [This applies to] what is to be eaten, what is to be consumed, and beds and seats.

"Sarvau" means of all these; even that samādhi which has been explained, such as the "mind-circle arising from the flow of phenomena" (dharmadrava), has but a single nature, namely, bodhicitta. Now, since this manifested Vajrasattva possesses form, how is he to be perceived? To this, he says: "Buddha," and so forth. This [mantra] consists of four syllables as its feet. At the beginning of "abhāva," there is lengthening [to *abhhāva*]. By means of "buddhena"—that is, by way of awakening (*bodhana*)—he perceives everything; because his nature consists of the three [aspects of] body, speech, and mind, which are the forms of awakening (*bodhirūpa*), he is thus described. He is "made" and "seen" in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

What is the non-existence of all phenomena? It is so described because its nature (*svabhāva*) and essence (*prakṛti*) is a cognition equal to space; the meaning is that this is due to the non-existence of [objective] forms (*ākāra*). Vajra is the Holder of the Vajra (*vajradhara*); by him, the illusory nature (*māyā-svabhāva*) was taught, because it cannot be otherwise delimited. "They appear as having form while being equal to space" (*khasama honti paḍihāi sarūva*): because, while being equal to space, they manifest as possessing form. Others, however, do not recite the fourth quarter, saying that this consists of only three quarters. With the words beginning with *māyā*, he states the result.

In this [verse], the three groups of syllables are the feet; *dharma* is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). For one who defines the intrinsic nature of illusion, the "burden" previously established for the Vajra is the introduction to the *dharmakāya*, because that must necessarily be attained. He states the fault in the opposite case with the words beginning "existence" (*sattva*): he who conceives of existence as having the intrinsic nature of form and so forth possesses the intrinsic nature of a sentient being; for him, there is no method, that is, no *dharmakāya*.

Then one considers that very mind; for that mind as well, this alone is established as its essence and its proper nature, namely, its resemblance to an illusion, because mental forms (*ākāra*) are unreal. With reference to the expansion and withdrawal [of the mind], he says "ea" and so forth. The feet of these two [verses] consist of four syllables each. First, the mind is made like a mountain of *metu* (mercury/silver); by virtue of being elevated, vast, and radiant, it should not be too large, lest there be the risk of distraction, nor should it be too small, lest there be the risk of failing to achieve meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).

Thereafter, that mind arises as "purely enlightened" (*śuddhabuddha*), consisting solely of the Buddha because it is pervaded by the emanations of all the Tathāgatas. Subsequently, when that mind becomes weary, the mantra-practitioner withdraws it. When that withdrawal occurs, the practitioner recollects and meditates: through the withdrawal of all the Tathāgatas, he should discern his own mind as having the nature of Vajradhara.

Subsequently, one kindles the mind, equal to Mount Meru, in the form of a mass of light; within that heap of light, one moves [the mind] in the form of Vajrasattva by filling it with hundreds of thousands of millions of his bodies. Afterwards, one emanates the form of space through the gradual withdrawal of the bodies of the Vajradharas. Such is the nature of emanation and withdrawal—this is the conclusion. If it is argued that it is logical that only Tathāgatas emanate because they are withdrawn from other Tathāgatas, he says: "Sijjha," and so forth.

In this regard, when two odd-numbered triplets and two even-numbered triplets are joined within that mind, Vajrasattva is accomplished through the single flavor (*ekarasa*) of the withdrawal of all Tathāgatas; therefore, emanation (*spharaṇa*) is also logically established. By means of the phrase beginning with "stable" (*sthira*), [the text] states the time for emanation by Vajradhara: here, the two odd-numbered [breaths] consist of ten *mātrās* each, while the two even-numbered [breaths] consist of twelve *mātrās* each. The yogin emanates what is stable, but he should never emanate what is unstable.

In order to proclaim that accomplishment (*siddhi*) is easily attained in this tantra, he speaks the *dvipadī-ṣaṭka* beginning with "all" (*sabba*), and so forth. Here, the feet consist of three syllables (*trigaṇa*). "All is true" means that it has been spoken by me exactly according to the literal sound (*yathāruta*); "here" is the ellipsis. It is "accomplished" (*siddha*) because it is established by its very nature (*prakṛtisiddhatvāt*); "vehicle" (*yāna*) is the path to enlightenment; "with its own-being" (*sabhāvaṃ*) means together with reality (*sattatva*).

If it is argued that while this vehicle is established by nature, our mind is defiled, he says "citta" and so forth. This [verse] consists of two lines. Do not defile the mind, for it is equal to space because it is pure by nature; it is "equal" because there is no modification of that nature. How so? He says: because no impurity whatsoever stains it, for impurities are adventitious to that nature, like smoke, darkness, clouds, or frost in the sky. With the words "jāi" and so forth, he speaks of the power of the deity.

Here, the feet [of the verse] consist of three groups: "O yogins, this Blessed Lady Cundā, whose nature is primordial, gives birth to all Buddhas when her vajra-power is cultivated. "Power" (*prabhāva*) means manifestation or production. If she gives birth to the Buddhas, one might ask, "What is the need for Vajradhara? To this, he says: "The Goddess," and so forth. In this case, the feet [of the verse] consist of four groups.

The goddesses and the Vajra-holder deity possess one and the same nature, and these [goddesses] are its manifestations. To the question, "What then is the purpose of the Buddhas? he says: The Blessed Vajrasattva is the power (*prabhāva*), the manifestation (*vibhava*), and the essence (*sāra*) of the Buddhas themselves, because his nature is the Dharmakāya. For this very reason, he is the root of the Buddhas who are comprised within the two bodies (*kāya*).

And because the *dharmakāya* is without beginning or end, that alone is the root; thus, it is the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Buddhas of the three times as gathered by Vajradhara—this is the power of the deity (*devatābala*). He speaks of the power of intention (*āśayabala*) and the power of mantra (*mantrabala*) with the words beginning "anunaya" and so forth. *Anunaya* is the mental disposition toward the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings. Its cultivation is indicated by the third singular ending being replaced by "he"; and through that, accomplishment is certain, as is [accomplishment] by means of the syllable *hūṃ*, which signifies the sense of conciliation (*anunaya*).

Therefore, indicating that this very yoga must be practiced incessantly with undivided posture (*paryaṅka*), he says: *hiae a* and so forth. Here, the quarters consist of three *gaṇas*. There is also a long vowel at the end of the word *ūru*. [The thought] "my thigh pains, my foot pains"—this discursive thought regarding the thigh and foot (*ūrupādavitarka*) is futile because it obstructs the fruit, or it is delusion (*moha*) because it arises from ignorance (*ajñāna*). That [thought] is not to be made in the heart; it is not fit to be performed in the heart.

One might object: "Since there are obstacles (vighnas), how can there be accomplishment? To this he says "vajra," and so forth. The lords of beings in the ten directions—Indra, Agni, Nairṛta, and the others—are accompanied by their retinues and are the destroyers of obstacles. The "wheel" (cakra) of the three worlds is their assembly; it is "restrained" by the splendors of the vajra. The "splendors of the vajra" (vajraprabhā) are the rays issuing from the vajra at the heart, which, as they flash forth, take the form of blazing vajras. By these [splendors] it is restrained—that is, dispelled. Therefore, the sense is that obstacles have no power here.

If it is argued that the destruction of obstacles through the yogas of the wrathful deities is more powerful, he says: "PHĀRA," and so forth. Here too, there are three syllables for each foot. The yogin expands thousands of millions of wrathful deities of the celestial realm; with the conviction (*adhimokṣa*) of non-difference from Vajradhara, he then necessarily reabsorbs them as having the very nature of the vajra. And because this tantra primarily concerns the meaning of being equal to space (*khasama*), it is designated by that very name.

Therefore, in order to summarize that very point, he says "of the mind" (*citta*) and so forth. This is a double-path [verse]. The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the fundamental state (*prakṛti*), and suchness (*tathatā*) belong to the mind. Awakening (*bodhi*) is the way (*naya*) of that very [mind], not of the stains. Therefore, when those [stains] are exhausted, because it is inexhaustible, awakening is easily attained.

Now, one might ask: "Enlightenment (*bodhi*) is infinite, yet the Buddha-qualities (*buddhadharma*) are [also] infinite; how then can they be its reality (*tattva*)? To this he says, "The method of enlightenment," and so forth. The method of enlightenment is reality, which is precisely the intrinsic nature of the mind (*cittasvabhāva*), that is, the suchness of the mind (*cittatathatā*). For that alone is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Buddhas, because it is the basis (*āśraya*) of the Buddha-qualities; it is not, however, the Buddha-qualities themselves. For those are its manifestations (*vibhava*), not its essential nature (*svarūpa*). If, then, suchness alone is the reality of both, and that is emptiness (*śūnyatā*), the absence of duality—

Because duality is always and everywhere non-existent, it is absolutely absent, like a rabbit’s horn. Furthermore, absolute non-existence cannot be the intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) of phenomena, nor can there be a direct perception (*pratyakṣībhāva*) of that [nature], because its essence is non-luminous. Therefore, he says "both," and so forth. "Both" refers to the thought of awakening (*bodhicitta*) and awakening (*bodhi*); their intrinsic nature is suchness (*tathatā*). The "mind" (*citta*) regarding that is the method (*naya*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The mind itself, devoid of duality, is the emptiness of duality; this is indicated by the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) applied to that which consists of nothing but that.

If, then, mind itself is emptiness, and since the mind is from the very beginning deluded—its very nature being such—then delusion itself would be awakening (*bodhi*). But that is incorrect, because awakening is the moment of the complete exhaustion of all delusions along with their latent predispositions (*vāsanā*). Therefore, regarding this "awakening," he says: "O, mind! and so forth. For delusion and its objective signs are merely adventitious stains.

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the mind, however, is indeed like space because it is mere luminosity; for mental aspects (*ākāra*) are non-existent, being sometimes perceived through their disappearance and sometimes through their very non-existence. In the states of mind—whether mundane, supramundane, or subsequently attained—it is precisely because adventitious stains (*āgantuka-mala*) are [removable] that awakening is easily attained, respectively. Therein, the purification of adventitious stains is what is to be accomplished, whereas natural purity (*prakṛti-śuddhi*) is already established.
This chapter elucidates the common meaning found in other tantras and in various chapters.
By this merit, which has attained a beauty as lovely as the autumnal moonlight, that I have acquired through speech by worshipping the glorious *Khasama* Tantra,
may I swiftly attain the peerless Brahman, which is equal to space and beyond compare.
Wherein the union of the lights of the qualities prevails for the sake of the universe.
The fifth chapter in the commentary on the Khasamatantra, titled the Khasamā.
And this commentary, titled *Khasamā*, is completed. This work is the composition of the great scholar, the venerable Ratnakaraśānti.
